content: 1. The Roman festival Parentalia, held from February 13 to 21, was dedicated to honoring the ancestors of the family. 2. The Roman festival Lemuria, observed on May 9, 11, and 13, was associated with the fear of active ghosts (larvae). During this time, the head of the household (pater familias) would attempt to appease these spirits by offering beans. 3. In ancient Rome, burials or cremations within the city were prohibited for both sacred and civil reasons. This was to prevent priests from being ritually contaminated by contact with a corpse and to avoid the risk of houses catching fire from funeral pyres. 4. Over time, various lawmakers imposed restrictions on the length, extravagance, cost, and conduct of funerals and mourning practices. 5. In Roman society, the pomp and duration of funeral rites were often politically or socially motivated, serving to advertise or elevate the status of a particular family or kin group. 6. Such ostentatious displays were considered harmful to society, leading to the establishment of regulations for mourning. For example, some laws prohibited women from loud wailing or self-mutilation, and limits were placed on spending for tombs and burial garments. 7. Romans frequently constructed their own tombs during their lifetimes, as evidenced by inscriptions such as V.F. (Vivus Fecit) or V.S.P. (Vivus Sibi Posuit), meaning Made while alive or Placed for himself while alive. 8. 9. Hypogea featured niches carved into the walls to hold urns, resembling pigeonholes, which were called columbaria. 10. In the Scottish Highlands, an old funeral custom involved burying the deceased with a wooden plate on their chest. 11. The plate contained a small amount of earth and salt, symbolizing the future of the deceased. The earth represented the body’s return to the soil, while the salt symbolized the soul, which does not decay. This practice was known as earth laid upon a corpse. 12. Between 1600 and 1914, two now largely forgotten professions existed in Europe: the funeral mute and the professional mourner. 13. Funeral mutes, often depicted in art and literature (e.g., Charles Dickens' Oliver Twist), were hired to stand silently at funerals with a sorrowful expression. 14. Professional mourners, usually women, would cry, wail, and sometimes claw at their faces or tear their clothing to encourage others to grieve. 15. This practice was common in ancient Greek plays and throughout Europe but largely disappeared by the 19th century, though it persists in parts of Africa and the Middle East. 16. The 2003 Philippine comedy Crying Ladies portrays the lives of part-time professional mourners in Manila’s Chinatown, where the Chinese community employs them to create the impression that the deceased was well-loved, expediting their soul’s entry into heaven. 17. Viking chieftains were traditionally placed in ships after death, along with tools and weapons. 18. These ships were set ablaze and sent out to sea, a practice still reenacted in northern European festivals like Up Helly-Aa and the Delamont Viking Festival. 19. Military heroes such as Nelson, Wellington, and Sir Winston Churchill had their coffins paraded through London on gun carriages, originally pulled by horses but now by sailors, in what is known as a State Funeral. 20. Some cultures inter the dead in tombs, either individually or in designated burial grounds. 21. In areas with high groundwater levels, above-ground tombs are used, as seen in New Orleans, Louisiana. 22. Separate buildings for tombs, often reserved for the wealthy or socially prominent, are called mausoleums. 23. Crypts within churches also serve as tombs, typically for the socially elite, though hygiene laws have restricted this practice in modern times. 24. In some regions, burial grounds are reused due to limited space. Once bodies decompose to skeletons, the bones are removed and placed in ossuaries. 25. This is common in naval traditions, with specific funeral services included in the Church of England’s Book of Common Prayer. 26. Science fiction often draws parallels to burial in space. 27. Cremation is an ancient practice, common in ancient Rome and Greece, where graves were often marked with mounds. Vikings occasionally cremated their dead in longships, marking the site with standing stones. 28. Despite objections from some religious groups, cremation has become increasingly common in recent years. 29. Orthodox Judaism, the Eastern Orthodox Church, and most Muslims forbid cremation. Orthodox Judaism believes cremation prevents the soul from finding its final repose. 30. The Roman Catholic Church forbade cremation for many years but has allowed it since 1963, provided it is not done to deny belief in bodily resurrection. Cremated remains must be buried or entombed, not scattered or kept at home. 31. Many Catholic cemeteries now include columbarium niches or specific sections for cremated remains. 32. Some Protestant denominations permit cremation, though conservative groups generally do not. 33. Hindus consider the funeral the final samskar or life ritual. Cremation is mandatory for most Hindus, except for saints and children under five. 34. Cremation satisfies the five elements of fire, water, earth, air, and space, as ashes are poured into the sacred Ganges River or the sea. 35. After death, the body is placed on the ground with the head pointing south, the direction of the dead. 36. The body is anointed with sacred items like sandalwood paste, holy ashes, tulsi leaves, and water from the Ganges. 37. The eldest son whispers sacred mantras near the deceased’s ear, such as Om Namah Shivaya or Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya. 38. An oil lamp is lit beside the deceased, and chapters from the Bhagavad Gita or Garuda Purana are recited. 39. Traditionally, the body must be cremated within 24 hours to avoid impurity and facilitate the soul’s passage to the afterlife.
